metadata.title: The Black Box Problem
metadata.purpose: STEM & AI Architecture, Week 13 — human-in-the-loop architecture: what oversight buys that automation cannot, what a governance dashboard has to show to make a reviewer effective, how confirmed failures become regression tests, and why the escalation router decides the whole value of the design.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Onkar Bhujbal. You would not get into a self-driving car with no windshield and no brake pedal. And yet autonomous agents get deployed into finance, healthcare and legal work every day with no window onto what the model is actually saying, and no way for anyone to stop it mid-decision. Today: human-in-the-loop architecture, and what a governance dashboard has to do to count as a steering wheel.

beats.narration_text: Pure automation is excellent for throughput and terrible for accountability. In a high-stakes domain you cannot let a model grade its own homework indefinitely, because the failure mode is confident and quiet. Human-in-the-loop pairs automated guardrails with human judgement: the machine clears routine traffic at machine speed, and the cases that could do damage stop and wait for a person. Speed on the volume, judgement on the exposure.

beats.honesty_note: The 99/1 split is the script's own illustration and is shown as a code comment rather than asserted as a measured rate. The $4.5M / $450K figures reuse this project's running example.

beats.narration_text: A governance dashboard is not a wall of charts — it is a decision surface, and a reviewer needs exactly three things on it. Live system health, so they know the pipeline itself is up. A side-by-side of what the model claimed against the verified source, because nobody can adjudicate a claim without the evidence next to it. And a filterable audit trail, so the decision can be defended later. Three zones, no hierarchy between them.

beats.narration_text: The part that makes this compound is what happens after the click. A reviewer confirms a hallucination, and that payload does not just get blocked — it becomes a permanent regression case. Months later, someone updates a prompt or swaps an embedding model, that case runs in C.I., and the merge is refused. The reviewer's judgement from last March is still enforcing itself without anyone remembering it was ever made.

beats.honesty_note: neverArms is set because this beat narrates a BLOCKED merge. Case numbers and dates are illustrative. The CI framing deliberately connects to the Week 7 and Week 10 reels, where the gate itself was built.

beats.narration_text: So where does this break? Two places, and neither is the dashboard. First, the router. Something has to decide which cases are dangerous enough to escalate, and that something is part of the system being checked — so anything it misreads as routine is never seen by a human at all. Your oversight covers the failures you already knew how to recognise. Second, volume. Give a reviewer two hundred escalations an hour and they will approve them, because that is what a queue does to a person. At that point the human is not deciding; they are absorbing liability for a decision the machine already made.

beats.authoring_note: BEAT ADDED. The script treats the 99/1 escalation split as a solved parameter. Two failures are named: SELECTION (the escalation classifier is inside the trust boundary, so unknown failure modes never surface) and VOLUME (automation bias — a reviewer under queue pressure rubber-stamps, converting oversight into liability transfer). The named mitigations are random sampling of the routine path and a hard cap on queue rate.

beats.narration_text: So automate the scale and keep humans in charge of the truth — but audit the router, not just the queue. Sample what you auto-approved. That sample is the only place an unknown failure mode can show up.

props.code:
if risk == "routine":
    if random() < 0.01:       # audit sample
        queue_for_review(out, tag="sampled")
    return out

queue_for_review(out, tag="escalated")

# TASK: keep a human in the loop.

# The escalated queue finds what you
# expected. The sampled queue finds
# what you did not.
props.sparkLine: Audit the router, not just the queue.

beats.authoring_note: The 1% audit sample is the reel's addition and is the direct countermeasure to the selection failure in B05.

beats.narration_text: Here is the prompt worth running against your own system. Ask a model to describe the worst output it could produce that your escalation rules would classify as routine. Whatever it describes will never reach a reviewer, which makes it the only part of your pipeline with no oversight at all.
